set.approach: Drive the signed Davis Canyon road, which turns to high-clearance four-wheel-drive track within a short distance, and park where a track bends toward the foot of the talus cone; the tower stands west of the road. Do not take the southern line that heads into scrambling over the white rim. Instead aim for a break in the rim farther north, follow the rim along until you are below the east face, and finish up a passable trail over the last hump. Liquid Sky and the neighbouring roof crack are visible above as you arrive.
set.descent_text: From the summit, rappel south into the chimney and notch above the big roof, where an old bolt ladder sits; inspect it before trusting it. From the notch, rappel on three bolts of doubtful quality along the formation's west side to the ground, so back up or replace worn anchors if you can.
hazards: Squeeze chimney through a roof that is strongly dependent on body size and can stop a larger climber
Rappel bolts on the west side of the tower and the old bolt ladder in the notch are of doubtful quality
Long sections of offwidth and squeeze climbing that are strenuous and awkward to protect
Sandstone is fragile when wet and holds can break, so avoid climbing during or just after rain

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped: no page opened states them. Descent is the tower's normal descent as the area page describes it, not specific to this line.

set.approach: Continue past the Bridger Jack mesa and the two Sixshooter towers, then turn left onto the signed road into Davis Canyon. Several miles up this road, which needs high clearance, leave the vehicle in the dry creekbed at the easiest spot on the mesa where the road starts to leave it. A cairned trail climbs the mesa and keeps you off the fragile crust of soil; allow roughly an hour of steady uphill walking to reach the base of the tower.
hazards: The road up Davis Canyon needs high clearance and gets rough, so a vehicle can be stranded far from help
Sandstone breaks easily when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain
Long uphill walk-in with no facilities, so carry water and pack out waste
set.overview: A three-pitch trad line up the south side of the southern of the two Sixshooter sandstone towers near Indian Creek, in the Davis Canyon area. It is graded 5.7 with a point of aid noted, which makes it one of the more moderate ways onto a desert tower. The real effort is the long uphill walk to the base, and the summit gives a wide view over the canyon country.

review.notes: Descent skipped: the pages opened had none (other pages only seen as search summaries; they suggest a rappel of the face, not verified). Season, gain, distance skipped. Grade 5.7 is as the database holds it; some other listings call the normal line 5.6.

set.approach: Reach Taylor Canyon in Canyonlands National Park by the Mineral Bottom road and the steep descent to the Green River, then drive about five sandy miles up the canyon to the campsite. From the parking area just beyond the campsite, follow the obvious cairned trail that climbs the talus cone and reaches the tower's base. The walk is roughly a mile out and back, about an hour, with some 700 feet of climbing. Without a permit or high clearance you must instead hike down the Alcove Spring trail, which turns this into a very long day.
set.descent_text: Rappel the north face on short double-rope rappels, using the fixed anchors; the older stations there have been replaced with double bolts joined by a chain, but check each before committing. The descent down the south side is not obvious, so most parties come down the north side and then retrace the trail to the parking area.
hazards: Friable sandstone and potentially poor belay stances typical of desert towers
Tunnel pitch is a dark tight squeeze that a larger-chested climber may not fit through
Crux corner widens to an overhanging offwidth that needs many large cams and is strenuous at the top
Warm walk-in and strong gusts; sand and dust make camping unpleasant
Road down to the river is steep and washes out in storms, so skip it if rain or snow is forecast

review.notes: Rappel count omitted: one page says five short double-rope raps, another says four; they disagree. Gain and distance skipped: the park trail figures (1.3 mi round trip, 717 ft change) are to the base only. Season skipped.

set.approach: Zeus stands in Taylor Canyon beyond Moses. Drive down to the end of the canyon road past the campsite, take the cairned trail up the talus cone to Moses's base, and keep walking up the trail past Moses to reach Zeus. The park trail is about a mile and a quarter out and back from the road.
set.descent_text: Rappel down the tower's northeast side, using the fixed anchors on the way down, and then walk back along the trail past Moses to the parking area. Two ropes are needed to reach the ground in the longest rappel.
hazards: Third pitch crux is poorly protected and a fall would land on the ledge below
Several pitches rely on old drilled pins and belay anchors of uneven quality
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain
set.overview: A three-pitch, 250-foot trad route up the south face of Zeus, a sandstone tower in Taylor Canyon on the Island in the Sky. It follows a dihedral on the left side of the face, with a finger crack and drilled pins on the first pitch, a strenuous thin lieback crack on the second, and a poorly protected 5.11 crux on the third. The R rating is earned on that final pitch, where a fall would hit a ledge.

review.notes: Rappel stated as one long (about 200 ft) rappel by one page only; text says two ropes needed without a count. Approach reuses Moses parking since the Zeus page just says walk past Moses. Season, gain, distance skipped.

set.descent_text: Rappel the line of ascent from the summit ridge, using the bolted belay stations and drilled angles, and then walk out the way you came in. Avoid the loose sandy ramp variation on the final pitch when pulling ropes.
hazards: Rock is weathered and looser than on neighbouring Moses, with blocks that can pull off
Loose sand on the ramp variation to the plank ledge
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain
set.overview: A four-pitch trad route on Aphrodite, a slender tower in Taylor Canyon on the Island in the Sky. It climbs ledges and an offwidth dihedral on the south face to reach the east ridge, then follows the ridge to the summit. The single 5.10c move comes on the third pitch, and the rock is more weathered than on neighbouring Moses.

review.notes: Approach skipped: page has none (Aphrodite lies up Taylor Canyon beyond Zeus but no opened page states the walk). Season, gain, distance skipped.

set.approach: Follow the Island in the Sky road to Monument Basin and, where it bends due south near the rim, walk out on bare rock to the edge, staying off the fragile crust of soil. Set up an anchor, fix a rope and rappel to the ground, and bring ascenders to climb the rope on the way out. Then follow the small wash down into the basin to the tower rather than cutting across the crust.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route: two 60 m ropes reach from the summit anchors to the top of pitch two, then rappel to the top of pitch one and again to the ground. After that, hike out the wash and climb the fixed rope back to the rim.
hazards: Belay ledges are small and very exposed, and the second pitch belay is hanging and awkward
The elephant-ear flake on pitch three may detach, and the crux hold could break
Fixed rope out of the basin must be climbed with ascenders at the end of the day
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain
set.overview: The original line up Standing Rock, a slender 300-foot sandstone tower in Monument Basin on the Island in the Sky, first climbed in 1962 and freed in 1993. Four pitches lead from a steep dihedral and roof, through a long sustained crack system with several moderate 5.10 moves, to a short burly crux protected by bolts. The summit is flat and holds a register.

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped (no page states them).

set.approach: Drive the Potash road to the Shafer and White Rim junction, then follow the White Rim road to a parking area on slickrock beneath the towers. Hike up the canyon until a trail leaves to the left toward the towers. From there either head for the Washer Woman and Monster Tower saddle, which needs some easy fifth-class climbing from steep talus on the south side, or contour around the base of Monster Tower to the west face where the route starts.
set.descent_text: Rappel the line of the Kor Route with two ropes. The first rappel returns to the base of the last pitch, onto its ledge, the second goes through the arch and hangs free down the face to bolted anchors, and with two 60 m ropes the third reaches the ground. Otherwise stop at one of the other sets of bolts to rappel again.
hazards: Loose rock on the first pitch and rotten bands on the final pitch, with a runout 5.9 section
Free-hanging rappel through the arch is exposed and getting over the edge is intimidating
Loose rock may be dislodged when pulling ropes on the second rappel
Sandy, sloping holds where the chimney on pitch two exits
Long drive on rough White Rim road and a scrambling approach to the saddle

review.notes: Rappel count stated as two to three by the page itself, so I described the sequence without a number. Season, gain, distance skipped.

set.approach: Park on the road southwest of the towers just before the wash where the road turns left, pulling as far off the road as you can. Head up the ridgeline just north of the parking, climb the benches to the final talus slope, then traverse from the south end of Monster Tower around to the east side, just below the notch between the towers, where the route begins.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route on single-rope rappels with a 70 m rope, using the fixed anchors found atop each pitch. Hang on to the line you climbed so the ropes do not snag on the ridge, and return down the approach path to the parking area.
hazards: Fourth pitch carries the most loose rock on the tower
Final pitch bulge and bolt ladder may need aid, with a summit that has no real anchor
Rangers warn against parking off the roadbed, so pull well clear
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain

review.notes: Another page (not opened) describes a multi-rappel descent, so no rappel count given. Season, gain, distance skipped.

set.approach: From Highway 313 on the Island in the Sky, turn onto the Mineral Bottom road and follow it to the switchbacks down to the river. Turn left along the river for a couple of miles to the park boundary, then zero your odometer and go 1.2 miles beyond the boundary. The towers show on your left, up a wash, and you walk up that wash to the base of the needle.

review.notes: Descent, hazards, season skipped: the only pages mentioning them were search summaries or a database mirror that returned 404 when opened. Approach covers the drive and the wash only, not the final climb up to the base.

set.approach: Start at the end of the main road in Arches National Park, in the Devils Garden parking area. Follow the main trail to Landscape Arch, continue onto the Primitive Loop, and look for the signed spur just south of Double O Arch that leads to the spire. The approach is about two miles each way past several arches and needs moderate scrambling in places; stay on established trails and washes and off the fragile ground crust.

review.notes: Distance skipped: one page says about 2 miles, the other 4.9 round trip, which differ by more than 10%. Descent, hazards, season skipped: no opened page gives them for this route (rappel details only seen in search summaries).

set.approach: From the Arches visitor center drive 9.3 miles and turn right onto the Windows road. After 1.1 miles, the Garden of Eden parking area is on the left; Owl Rock is the spire to the east-southeast, only about 200 feet from the start. Use established trails and avoid the fragile ground crust, and reach the base by the west ramp rather than the crumbly steps on the north side.
set.descent_text: Downclimb about ten feet from the top to the anchor just below the summit and rappel the route. A single 60 m rope is long enough to reach the ground from this anchor.
hazards: Crumbly sandy steps along the ramp's north side carry a groundfall of about twenty feet
Busy tower, so groups may queue at the base on weekends
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain
set.overview: A short, popular 5.8 trad crack that climbs the obvious west side of Owl Rock, a sandstone spire beside the Garden of Eden parking area in Arches National Park. It is quick to reach and quick to finish, with sustained crack climbing that suits hands and fingers well, and the summit is only a short downclimb from the anchor.

review.notes: Season skipped (one page says any season, summers hot; not a window). Gain and distance not needed for a 200 ft walk-in.

set.approach: The parking lot sits at the north end of the Courthouse Wash trail. Walk the trail a few minutes until you are level with Argon Tower, then follow intermittent climbers' trails around the north end of the tower. These lead past the lower part of the tower to a bench on its west side, ten to fifteen minutes from the lot.
set.descent_text: Rappel the west face from the top of the fourth pitch. Two 60 m ropes may reach the ground in one rappel, but be ready to stop at a midway anchor and rappel again if you cannot see the ground.
hazards: Sandy, soft rock; a placed cam can be hard to remove
Poorly protected and loose holds on the upper corner pitch
Finish relies on a bolt ladder that is climbed on aid
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped. Pitch count on the route page is five whereas the database overview says four; I avoided giving a count.
